How to play

The goal is to target human review where the AI needs help. You succeed when all six usable moments reach the album, no spoiled shots get through, and you use no more than 3 editor checks.

Read the deck from left to right. Higher scores mean the AI is more confident a shot is usable. Confidence is imperfect: a high-scoring shot can still be spoiled. Scores are simulated, not probability percentages.

Gates are decision thresholds, score cutoffs on the AI’s ranking. Shots below the check gate are discarded, and shots at or above the keep gate go straight into the album. Drag a gate, or focus it and use the arrow keys, Home or End.

Target your editor checks at the doubtful shots between the gates, while the AI handles the rest. The editor keeps only usable shots. Releasing a gate runs the edit and checks the album and review budget automatically.

Stacks marked 28 shots group repeated outtakes. Every shot in a stack counts and needs its own check.

Balanced sample keeps one shot per stack. Switch to it to compare the AI’s accuracy, precision and recall at the same gates.

Why high accuracy can still miss moments

The AI gives every shot a score, and the contact sheet ranks the roll from lower to higher score. A decision threshold turns that score into a decision. The keep gate is the AI’s threshold: at or above it the AI predicts usable, and below it the AI predicts unusable. The metrics in the game describe the AI alone at that cutoff, before any editor checks.

On the full roll, usable shots are the rare class: 6 of 120, or 5%. A rule that rejects everything still scores 95% accuracy and delivers an empty album. On the balanced sample, which keeps one shot per stack, the same rule scores 50%. The extra easy rejects lift accuracy without finding a single moment, so accuracy can look high while moments are missing.

Precision is the share of the AI’s keeps that are usable: TP / (TP + FP). Recall is the share of usable shots the AI keeps: TP / (TP + FN). Accuracy is (TP + TN) divided by all shots. A true positive (TP) is a usable shot kept, a false positive (FP) is a spoiled shot kept, a false negative (FN) is a usable shot missed and a true negative (TN) is a spoiled shot rejected. Precision is undefined when nothing is kept. Lowering the keep gate can only raise or hold recall, while precision may fall as spoiled shots come in.

The check gate adds a person to the decision. Shots between the gates go to an editor, who keeps only the usable ones. The challenge assesses where you target that limited review: all six usable shots must reach the album, no spoiled shots may pass, and the checks must fit the budget. Editor checks change the album but leave the AI’s scores and metrics as they were. You improve the outcome by choosing where a person intervenes.

Explore in Deep Learning: precision, recall and choosing a decision rule for the cost of mistakes.

The AI scores and photo labels are authored for this puzzle, and the concert photos are generated. Scores are simulated and are not probabilities, and no model runs on your device. Usable means the subject is visible and sharp enough. On the full roll, four low-score stacks each stand for 28 spoiled shots that share the pictured defect and score. Editors work from left to right, a stack uses one check per shot, and extra shots wait in the queue. Any pair of gates that meets the goal counts. These are grouped examples, not 120 distinct photographs or a measured model benchmark.
